items.text:
Every time I see a meat tenderizer, I think of my mother. Specifically of the way in which she, as someone wary of emotional vulnerability yet full of affection (classic Boomer combo), decided to make Austrian pork schnitzel her love language — and the meat tenderizer her translator. In hindsight, that steel hammer was one of the best, most essential cooking tools in our home; it was also a beginner-friendly tool for me, a Montessori kid used to playing with saws at recess and expressing my feelings via dried bean art.

That tenderizer has become a staple of my kitchen ecosystem today. But one person’s tenderizer is another’s hand-me-down whisk, Japanese chef’s knife, or grill press. So what do other people consider their ride-or-die cooking tools? What are the baseline peelers, knives, and spatulas that are in constant rotation, the tools that make you feel like a culinary John Wick? I decided to ask not just chefs, but chefs with culinary school teaching experience (aka endless patience and a knowledge of novice-level skillsets) about what they consider to be the best beginner cooking tools.

In addition to a few of my own cooking essentials, I picked the brains of four teachers with experience in a variety of programs, from Hot Bread Kitchen — a New York City nonprofit that helps immigrants break into the food industry — to the legendary Institute of Culinary Education, all in the hopes of answering the inherently relative question of what constitutes an essential cooking tool for beginners.

Whether or not your new kitchen workhorse is destined to become an heirloom, some dos and don’ts for your search…

Do: Look for tools that don’t just do one thing.

Do: Read product reviews.

Don’t: Spend more than you need to on, say, a pair of tongs. And if you’re lucky enough to have a grandpa with a sick filet knife, maybe ask him about it.

First, grab a meat tenderizer.


Kitexpert Meat Tenderizer

Where to Buy:

$14.99 $11.98 at Amazon


Now, let’s talk essentials.

The best beginner cooking tools, according to Hot Bread Kitchen culinary teachers

Hot Bread Kitchen is a NYC-based culinary institute whose goal is to “uplift women, gender-expansive people, immigrants, and people of color” by helping them launch their careers in the food industry through intensive culinary training. Culinary instructors Kandy Williams and Charlene Johnson are two of the organization’s many acclaimed teachers, and they had some choice advice on the best beginner cooking tools.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Hot Bread Kitchen (@hotbreadkitchen)


A great spatula

“Spatulas are often one of the first tools that I introduce to my kids to learn to use when cooking because they’re safe and easy to handle,” says Williams. “It’s your all-in-one tool — perfect for flipping, stirring, and scraping every bit of batter from a bowl.”

“I love to use a silicone spatula to gently fold ingredients like egg whites into batter,” Williams goes on. “As a baker, this is one of my favorite tools in the kitchen. I use it all the time when I prepare my buttercreams, cakes, and alfajores (Peruvian macarons). This keeps the mixture light and fluffy.”

Johnson seconds the tool’s utility for not only whipping up meals, but also allowing you to store your leftovers and ingredients. “It will allow you to get every bit of your food from containers,” she says, “to where they need to be — in your belly!”

Reach for a BPA-free silicone spatula such as this high-rated option that costs less than an order of avocado toast. It’s heat-resistant up to 600 degrees Fahrenheit, has a stainless steel internal frame — just like RoboCop — and a slightly curved blade for scraping and folding with precision.


DI ORO Silicone Spatula

Where to Buy:

$13.97 at Amazon


A workhouse vegetable peeler

At home, Williams relies on a high-quality peeler to prep everything from mashed potatoes to causa peruana with her kids; it makes prep work much faster for her students and more efficient for her as a culinary instructor. “I always show how to use a peeler safely by peeling away from the body and using short, controlled strokes. They use it to peel potatoes, carrots, butternut squash, and more vegetables. It’s also a great tool to introduce them to different textures.”

Johnson also swears by the power of the classic Swiss peeler, specifically — and not just for veggies. “It’s efficient and precise,” she says. “Use it on chocolate, cheese, or citrus. Get creative. FYI, the purpose of the protruding circle to the side of the peeler is to remove potato eyes.”

Williams Sonoma’s straight swivel-action, steel blade peeler contours to the shape of whatever potato, pear, or state fair butter sculpture you’re peeling:


Williams Sonoma Prep Tools Straight Swivel Peeler

Where to Buy:

$22.95 at Williams Sonoma


For a classic Swiss peeler, you can’t go wrong with a Victorinox straight blade, which has been GOATed by many. It’s peeler is lightweight, is made with a nonslip textured handle, and is under $10 on Amazon.


Victorinox straight-blade peeler

Where to Buy:

$9 at Amazon


A solid paring knife

As Williams says, a paring knife is “small and versatile, perfect for tasks that require precision, like peeling, trimming, or slicing small fruits and veggies.” She introduces the tool to beginner students to use for more delicate tasks — such as cutting strawberries, scoring tomatoes, or trimming herbs — in order to build their knife skills safely. “In classes my students use a paring knife to practice the concasse technique,” she says, “They love to prepare ratatouille. The paring knife is often called the ‘extension of the hand’ because it’s so maneuverable.”

Quality knives can be a costly investment, but beginners will appreciate the affordable paring knife from Quince. Its 3.5-inch paring knife is made out of 33 layers of Japanese Damascus stainless steel — which helps it achieve excellent blade balance — and it features a naturally water-resistant Pakkawood handle.


Quince Essential Japanese Damascus steel 3.5” paring knife

Where to Buy:

$39.9 at Quince


An offset serrated knife

Johnson says her serrated knife is key for cutting bread, slicing tomatoes, and more. “It’s great for anything that has a tough exterior and soft interior,” she explains. “The offset handle provides space so that the blade hits the cutting board before my hand. Efficient and delivers stellar results. 10 out of 10.”

This 9-inch offset blade sports an ergonomic handle and a serrated blade that does the job of the fancier versions at an entry-level price.


Mercer Culinary Offset Bread Knife

Where to Buy:

$27.99 at Amazon


The best beginner cooking tools, according to Celine Beitchman of the Institute of Culinary Education

The Institute of Culinary Education (ICE) was founded in 1975, and is ranked as the number-one culinary school in the United States, with locations in New York City and Los Angeles. Celine Beitchman, director of nutrition, tells me that she has been “teaching health-promoting culinary arts for about a decade,” and “became a chef over a 20-year period working in prep kitchens, restaurants, catering, and as a private chef,” first at the Natural Gourmet Institute and now within ICE’s Plant-Based Culinary Arts program.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Institute of Culinary Education (@iceculinary)


A big, sharp chef’s knife

If you don’t know where to begin with your own knife drawer, Beitchman recommends starting with an 8- to 10-inch chef’s knife. As she says, “It’s vital to handle most of the essential vegetable cuts, and for slicing everything from cheese to cake. A good knife will last, and it’s worth investing in one that you are comfortable using — one that’s not too long or heavy for you.” Check out our full guide to the best chef’s knives here, for every budget and purpose.

One of my first kitchen knives was a Made In blade, and I remember thinking, Wow, so this is what it feels like to hold a knife with its own backbone. Or, maybe what I was feeling was the single rod of stainless steel that extends from tip to handle, which is what the brand claims sets it apart. Years later, my 8-inch Made In chef’s knife still chops everything from crunchy cabbage to a tarte tatin with ease, despite my less-than-perfect knife skills.


Made In 8-inch chef’s knife

Where to Buy:

$129 $99.99 at Made In


If you’re shopping on more of a budget, I also can’t recommend Imarku’s chef’s knife enough. This 8-inch stainless steel blade cuts with as much precision as some of my friends’ fancy Wüsthof knives, but it costs under $50. I do need to sharpen it more frequently than some pricier knives (I find that the sweet spot is around every two months), but you really can’t beat the bang for your buck on this sucker. Plus, it ships in a secure, velvet-esque-lined box that makes for a thoughtful (last-minute) housewarming gift.


Imarku Japanese Chef’s Knife (8-Inch)

Where to Buy:

$39.99 at Amazon


Spring-loaded tongs

“Spring-loaded tongs with metal or rubber-coated tips can be used to toss salads in dressings or vegetables in seasonings before they hit the oven,” says Beitchman. “When I started cooking, tongs were almost an extension of my own hand and they let me reach further down the stove or up to the salamander.”

These stainless 12-inch long steel tongs come from one of my favorite affordable cookware brands, OXO. Scalloped edges are a big plus for me when it comes to tongs, because they allow for better precision and grip when I’m flipping whole padrón peppers on the grill or prodding my veggies around in a skillet. Plus, the slight concave of the tongs make it easy to ladle excess oils or sauce from a pan, (which I love to do when I’m frying eggs in chile crisp).


Oxo stainless steel tongs

Where to Buy:

$14.99 at Wayfair


Bench scraper

Finally, Beitchman stands by the power of the bench scraper. “[Bench scrapers] are amazingly versatile,” she says, “and can be used to move and lift food off of cutting boards and trays, to scrape flours and shape loaves before baking,” and more.

Crate & Barrel has gone the extra mile with this stainless steel bench scraper, which includes not only a soft-touch plastic handle that won’t slip from your grip, but a sweet little built-in ruler. It’s always a plus when a kitchen staple can combine more than one tool or function, and being able to measure out and chop your dough with one hand is a clutch time saver.


Crate & Barrel bench scraper

Where to Buy:

$19.95 at Crate & Barrel


The best beginner cooking tools, according to chef Vanessa Seder

Vanessa Seder has worked as a chef, food stylist, cookbook author, and associate food editor at Ladies’ Home Journal — to name just a handful of her culinary accomplishments — in addition to teaching for many years at the storied Stonewall Kitchen Headquarters in York, Maine. She, too, sang the praises of sharp chef’s knives and different-sized spatulas, but she also recommended a few more less-obvious tools.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Vanessa Seder (@vanessa_seder_eats)


A high-quality wood cutting board

It seems easy enough to remember, but a quality cutting board can sometimes go overlooked when you’re outfitting your kitchen with beginner cooking tools and equipment. Seder recommends John Boos & Co., one of the oldest manufacturers of butcher blocks in the country. She says that she loves the sturdy feel of her Boos board, which is 1.5 inches thick and perfect for rolling out dough while baking or making pasta, and also gives the board a bit of a height boost — a plus that she appreciates, she says, given that she’s on the taller side and doesn’t want to slouch while chopping or rolling herbs. It’s also quite a looker in terms of items that can take up precious real estate on your kitchen counters. As Seder says, “I use it sometimes as a cheese platter when we have guests over.”


John Boos Cutting Board (20” x 15”, Cherry Wood)

Where to Buy:

$158.95 at Amazon


A whetstone for sharpening knives

Those paring and chef’s knives aren’t going to sharpen themselves. As Seder says, “Learning how to sharpen your knives will save you money and time in the long run. A sharp knife is safer to use in that it prevents slippage, which can result in injury.” But getting your knives sharpened professionally can really add up in cost, she adds, so throwing down for a whetstone can be a great long-term investment. Consider this Japanese-made ceramic whetstone by King, which only costs about $50. There’s a dedicated Eater guide to sharpening your knives like a pro, but suffice to say this kit comes with everything you need: a 1000/6000 grit combination whetstone (with the former for main sharpening and the latter for finish sharpening), an angle holder for blade-sharpening accuracy, and a quick-drying cloth.


King whetstone

Where to Buy:

$52.99 at Amazon


A fish spatula

Seder says that she still has her fish spatula from culinary school, a trusty Wüsthof that continues to go the distance. This 6.5-inch slotted fish spatula from the German brand is about more than just fish, and acts as a flexible tool for cooking not only fish, but anything delicate. The Wüsthof version has earned heaps of praise for its being lightweight, angled, and slotted, which allows excess oils to drain through when you’re moving things around. Or as one reviewer writes, “Sometimes it is the small things in life that give you the motivation to be a better cook.” Our thoughts exactly.


Wüsthof slotted fish spatula

Where to Buy:

$65 at Amazon

$65 at Wüsthof


One more bonus tip: Invest in stainless steel cookware

A canon event in becoming a (slightly more) serious home cook is graduating from whatever ragtag collection of nonstick pans you’ve been accumulating since sophomore year of college to a proper set of cookware that will stand the test of time. Look in any commercial kitchen, and you’ll see stainless steel, stainless steel, stainless steel. Why? Because stainless steel cookware is durable, versatile, and has great heat conductivity and retention.

That’s why we took our collaboration with Heritage Steel seriously; our high-quality, 5-ply stainless steel pans are ready to take on any and all cooking projects, from perfect pancakes to sunny-side-up eggs to seared salmon (in which case the spatula above will come in handy). The 12-inch pan is the perfect do-everything size, while the 3-quart saucier (which also comes with a lid) can cook pasta, poach eggs, and so much more.


Eater x Heritage Steel 12-Inch Fry Pan

Where to Buy:

$129.95 at Heritage Steel

Eater x Heritage Steel 3-Quart Saucier With Lid

Where to Buy:

$169.95 at Heritage Steel

In addition to a few of my own cooking essentials, I picked the brains of four teachers with experience in a variety of programs, from Hot Bread Kitchen — a New York City nonprofit that helps immigrants break into the food industry — to the legendary Institute of Culinary Education, all in the hopes of answering the inherently relative question of what constitutes an essential cooking tool for beginners.
Whether or not your new kitchen workhorse is destined to become an heirloom, some dos and don’ts for your search…
Do: Look for tools that don’t just do one thing.
Do: Read product reviews.
Don’t: Spend more than you need to on, say, a pair of tongs. And if you’re lucky enough to have a grandpa with a sick filet knife, maybe ask him about it.
First, grab a meat tenderizer.
Kitexpert Meat Tenderizer
Where to Buy:
$14.99 $11.98 at Amazon
Now, let’s talk essentials.
The best beginner cooking tools, according to Hot Bread Kitchen culinary teachers

Hot Bread Kitchen is a NYC-based culinary institute whose goal is to “uplift women, gender-expansive people, immigrants, and people of color” by helping them launch their careers in the food industry through intensive culinary training. Culinary instructors Kandy Williams and Charlene Johnson are two of the organization’s many acclaimed teachers, and they had some choice advice on the best beginner cooking tools.
View this post on Instagram
A post shared by Hot Bread Kitchen (@hotbreadkitchen)
A great spatula

“Spatulas are often one of the first tools that I introduce to my kids to learn to use when cooking because they’re safe and easy to handle,” says Williams. “It’s your all-in-one tool — perfect for flipping, stirring, and scraping every bit of batter from a bowl.”

“I love to use a silicone spatula to gently fold ingredients like egg whites into batter,” Williams goes on. “As a baker, this is one of my favorite tools in the kitchen. I use it all the time when I prepare my buttercreams, cakes, and alfajores (Peruvian macarons). This keeps the mixture light and fluffy.”

Johnson seconds the tool’s utility for not only whipping up meals, but also allowing you to store your leftovers and ingredients. “It will allow you to get every bit of your food from containers,” she says, “to where they need to be — in your belly!”

Reach for a BPA-free silicone spatula such as this high-rated option that costs less than an order of avocado toast. It’s heat-resistant up to 600 degrees Fahrenheit, has a stainless steel internal frame — just like RoboCop — and a slightly curved blade for scraping and folding with precision.
DI ORO Silicone Spatula
Where to Buy:
$13.97 at Amazon
A workhouse vegetable peeler

At home, Williams relies on a high-quality peeler to prep everything from mashed potatoes to causa peruana with her kids; it makes prep work much faster for her students and more efficient for her as a culinary instructor. “I always show how to use a peeler safely by peeling away from the body and using short, controlled strokes. They use it to peel potatoes, carrots, butternut squash, and more vegetables. It’s also a great tool to introduce them to different textures.”

Johnson also swears by the power of the classic Swiss peeler, specifically — and not just for veggies. “It’s efficient and precise,” she says. “Use it on chocolate, cheese, or citrus. Get creative. FYI, the purpose of the protruding circle to the side of the peeler is to remove potato eyes.”
Williams Sonoma’s straight swivel-action, steel blade peeler contours to the shape of whatever potato, pear, or state fair butter sculpture you’re peeling:
Williams Sonoma Prep Tools Straight Swivel Peeler
Where to Buy:
$22.95 at Williams Sonoma

For a classic Swiss peeler, you can’t go wrong with a Victorinox straight blade, which has been GOATed by many. It’s peeler is lightweight, is made with a nonslip textured handle, and is under $10 on Amazon.
Victorinox straight-blade peeler
Where to Buy:
$9 at Amazon
A solid paring knife

As Williams says, a paring knife is “small and versatile, perfect for tasks that require precision, like peeling, trimming, or slicing small fruits and veggies.” She introduces the tool to beginner students to use for more delicate tasks — such as cutting strawberries, scoring tomatoes, or trimming herbs — in order to build their knife skills safely. “In classes my students use a paring knife to practice the concasse technique,” she says, “They love to prepare ratatouille. The paring knife is often called the ‘extension of the hand’ because it’s so maneuverable.”

Quality knives can be a costly investment, but beginners will appreciate the affordable paring knife from Quince. Its 3.5-inch paring knife is made out of 33 layers of Japanese Damascus stainless steel — which helps it achieve excellent blade balance — and it features a naturally water-resistant Pakkawood handle.
Quince Essential Japanese Damascus steel 3.5” paring knife
Where to Buy:
$39.9 at Quince
An offset serrated knife

Johnson says her serrated knife is key for cutting bread, slicing tomatoes, and more. “It’s great for anything that has a tough exterior and soft interior,” she explains. “The offset handle provides space so that the blade hits the cutting board before my hand. Efficient and delivers stellar results. 10 out of 10.”
This 9-inch offset blade sports an ergonomic handle and a serrated blade that does the job of the fancier versions at an entry-level price.
Mercer Culinary Offset Bread Knife
Where to Buy:
$27.99 at Amazon
The best beginner cooking tools, according to Celine Beitchman of the Institute of Culinary Education

The Institute of Culinary Education (ICE) was founded in 1975, and is ranked as the number-one culinary school in the United States, with locations in New York City and Los Angeles. Celine Beitchman, director of nutrition, tells me that she has been “teaching health-promoting culinary arts for about a decade,” and “became a chef over a 20-year period working in prep kitchens, restaurants, catering, and as a private chef,” first at the Natural Gourmet Institute and now within ICE’s Plant-Based Culinary Arts program.
View this post on Instagram
A post shared by Institute of Culinary Education (@iceculinary)
A big, sharp chef’s knife

If you don’t know where to begin with your own knife drawer, Beitchman recommends starting with an 8- to 10-inch chef’s knife. As she says, “It’s vital to handle most of the essential vegetable cuts, and for slicing everything from cheese to cake. A good knife will last, and it’s worth investing in one that you are comfortable using — one that’s not too long or heavy for you.” Check out our full guide to the best chef’s knives here, for every budget and purpose.

One of my first kitchen knives was a Made In blade, and I remember thinking, Wow, so this is what it feels like to hold a knife with its own backbone. Or, maybe what I was feeling was the single rod of stainless steel that extends from tip to handle, which is what the brand claims sets it apart. Years later, my 8-inch Made In chef’s knife still chops everything from crunchy cabbage to a tarte tatin with ease, despite my less-than-perfect knife skills.
Made In 8-inch chef’s knife
Where to Buy:
$129 $99.99 at Made In

If you’re shopping on more of a budget, I also can’t recommend Imarku’s chef’s knife enough. This 8-inch stainless steel blade cuts with as much precision as some of my friends’ fancy Wüsthof knives, but it costs under $50. I do need to sharpen it more frequently than some pricier knives (I find that the sweet spot is around every two months), but you really can’t beat the bang for your buck on this sucker. Plus, it ships in a secure, velvet-esque-lined box that makes for a thoughtful (last-minute) housewarming gift.
Imarku Japanese Chef’s Knife (8-Inch)
Where to Buy:
$39.99 at Amazon
Spring-loaded tongs

“Spring-loaded tongs with metal or rubber-coated tips can be used to toss salads in dressings or vegetables in seasonings before they hit the oven,” says Beitchman. “When I started cooking, tongs were almost an extension of my own hand and they let me reach further down the stove or up to the salamander.”

These stainless 12-inch long steel tongs come from one of my favorite affordable cookware brands, OXO. Scalloped edges are a big plus for me when it comes to tongs, because they allow for better precision and grip when I’m flipping whole padrón peppers on the grill or prodding my veggies around in a skillet. Plus, the slight concave of the tongs make it easy to ladle excess oils or sauce from a pan, (which I love to do when I’m frying eggs in chile crisp).
Oxo stainless steel tongs
Where to Buy:
$14.99 at Wayfair
Bench scraper

Finally, Beitchman stands by the power of the bench scraper. “[Bench scrapers] are amazingly versatile,” she says, “and can be used to move and lift food off of cutting boards and trays, to scrape flours and shape loaves before baking,” and more.

Crate & Barrel has gone the extra mile with this stainless steel bench scraper, which includes not only a soft-touch plastic handle that won’t slip from your grip, but a sweet little built-in ruler. It’s always a plus when a kitchen staple can combine more than one tool or function, and being able to measure out and chop your dough with one hand is a clutch time saver.
Crate & Barrel bench scraper
Where to Buy:
$19.95 at Crate & Barrel
The best beginner cooking tools, according to chef Vanessa Seder

Vanessa Seder has worked as a chef, food stylist, cookbook author, and associate food editor at Ladies’ Home Journal — to name just a handful of her culinary accomplishments — in addition to teaching for many years at the storied Stonewall Kitchen Headquarters in York, Maine. She, too, sang the praises of sharp chef’s knives and different-sized spatulas, but she also recommended a few more less-obvious tools.
View this post on Instagram
A post shared by Vanessa Seder (@vanessa_seder_eats)
A high-quality wood cutting board

It seems easy enough to remember, but a quality cutting board can sometimes go overlooked when you’re outfitting your kitchen with beginner cooking tools and equipment. Seder recommends John Boos & Co., one of the oldest manufacturers of butcher blocks in the country. She says that she loves the sturdy feel of her Boos board, which is 1.5 inches thick and perfect for rolling out dough while baking or making pasta, and also gives the board a bit of a height boost — a plus that she appreciates, she says, given that she’s on the taller side and doesn’t want to slouch while chopping or rolling herbs. It’s also quite a looker in terms of items that can take up precious real estate on your kitchen counters. As Seder says, “I use it sometimes as a cheese platter when we have guests over.”
John Boos Cutting Board (20” x 15”, Cherry Wood)
Where to Buy:
$158.95 at Amazon
A whetstone for sharpening knives

Those paring and chef’s knives aren’t going to sharpen themselves. As Seder says, “Learning how to sharpen your knives will save you money and time in the long run. A sharp knife is safer to use in that it prevents slippage, which can result in injury.” But getting your knives sharpened professionally can really add up in cost, she adds, so throwing down for a whetstone can be a great long-term investment. Consider this Japanese-made ceramic whetstone by King, which only costs about $50. There’s a dedicated Eater guide to sharpening your knives like a pro, but suffice to say this kit comes with everything you need: a 1000/6000 grit combination whetstone (with the former for main sharpening and the latter for finish sharpening), an angle holder for blade-sharpening accuracy, and a quick-drying cloth.
King whetstone
Where to Buy:
$52.99 at Amazon
A fish spatula

Seder says that she still has her fish spatula from culinary school, a trusty Wüsthof that continues to go the distance. This 6.5-inch slotted fish spatula from the German brand is about more than just fish, and acts as a flexible tool for cooking not only fish, but anything delicate. The Wüsthof version has earned heaps of praise for its being lightweight, angled, and slotted, which allows excess oils to drain through when you’re moving things around. Or as one reviewer writes, “Sometimes it is the small things in life that give you the motivation to be a better cook.” Our thoughts exactly.
Wüsthof slotted fish spatula
Where to Buy:
$65 at Amazon
$65 at Wüsthof
One more bonus tip: Invest in stainless steel cookware

A canon event in becoming a (slightly more) serious home cook is graduating from whatever ragtag collection of nonstick pans you’ve been accumulating since sophomore year of college to a proper set of cookware that will stand the test of time. Look in any commercial kitchen, and you’ll see stainless steel, stainless steel, stainless steel. Why? Because stainless steel cookware is durable, versatile, and has great heat conductivity and retention.

That’s why we took our collaboration with Heritage Steel seriously; our high-quality, 5-ply stainless steel pans are ready to take on any and all cooking projects, from perfect pancakes to sunny-side-up eggs to seared salmon (in which case the spatula above will come in handy). The 12-inch pan is the perfect do-everything size, while the 3-quart saucier (which also comes with a lid) can cook pasta, poach eggs, and so much more.
Eater x Heritage Steel 12-Inch Fry Pan
Where to Buy:
$129.95 at Heritage Steel
Eater x Heritage Steel 3-Quart Saucier With Lid
Where to Buy:
$169.95 at Heritage Steel

items.title: Rethinking Japan’s Imperial Succession: Patriarchy and the Search for National Identity
items.summary: An unpopular amendment to Japan’s Imperial House Law has reignited the debate over rules limiting the imperial succession to male children in the male line.
items.text:
An unpopular amendment to Japan’s Imperial House Law has reignited the debate over rules limiting the imperial succession to male children in the male line. Citing historical demographic research, the author highlights the role of a flexible dual-lineage tradition in the imperial household and Japanese society as a whole.

Succession Dilemma

A controversial revision of the Imperial House Law was enacted in July, sparking criticism and debate among a sharply divided, but largely disapproving public.

To be clear, the Japanese emperor is not a ruling monarch with political power or the authority to govern. As stated in Article 1 of the Constitution, promulgated in the aftermath of World War II, the emperor is “the symbol of the State and of the unity of the People, deriving his position from the will of the people with whom resides sovereign power.” This situates Japan’s imperial institution in the category of symbolic monarchies, the weakest form of constitutional monarchy.

That said, Japan’s imperial throne resembles typical monarchies in the sense that it is hereditary. Article 2 of the Constitution states, “The Imperial Throne shall be dynastic and succeeded to in accordance with the Imperial House Law passed by the Diet.”

Herein lies the problem. Article 1 of the Imperial House Law, originally enacted in 1889, stipulates that “the Imperial Throne shall be succeeded to by a male offspring in the male line belonging to the Imperial Lineage.”

Over the course of Japanese history, eight women have occupied the imperial throne, accounting for 10 of Japan’s official imperial reigns. Nonetheless, the Imperial House Law enacted after the Meiji Restoration of 1868 prohibited the accession of female emperors. And even after the promulgation of a new, democratic Constitution following Japan’s defeat in World War II, this provision of the Imperial House Law remained unchanged.

This constraint has grown increasingly problematic in recent years, as the number of children born to the imperial family has dwindled. Emperor Naruhito (age 66) and his wife, Empress Masako (62), have only one child, Princess Aiko (24). This puts the emperor’s younger brother, Crown Prince Akishino (60) and Akishino’s son, Prince Hisahito (20), first and second in line to the throne, respectively. Thanks to the nephew, succession seemed assured for the time being, but with so few young men in the imperial household, the future was looking uncertain.

A Step Backward

In response, the government recently introduced and enacted an amendment permitting the imperial family to adopt male relatives from branches of the family that were stripped of their imperial status after World War II. The male offspring of such men will then become eligible to succeed to the throne in the absence of a closer male relative. While another new provision allows female members of the imperial family to retain their imperial status even after marriage (previously, they automatically became commoners), it does not extend the same status to the princess’s husband or children. In short, the path to the throne is legally closed not only to female members of the imperial family but also to their descendants.

In this matter, the government appears to be out of step with public opinion. The cabinet’s approval rating fell by between 5% and 11% immediately after enactment of the revised Imperial House Law according to most polls. Even a survey by the daily Yomiuri Shimbun, which leans toward the right, found a full 85% of respondents in favor of amending the law again to permit the accession of female emperors.

What about the response overseas? The dominant reaction in the mainstream and social media seems to be one of amazement at the persistence of such sexist attitudes. “How old-fashioned!” exclaims one representative post. Many also find it ironic that the legislation was submitted by the cabinet of Takaichi Sanae, Japan’s first female prime minister. “If women can hold the office of Prime Minister,” remarks one contributor, “there is no compelling reason why Princess Aiko should be excluded from imperial succession.”

To be sure, some of those active in the international discourse space defend the move—ostensibly from the standpoint of cultural relativism and respect for Japanese culture—in some cases, accusing critics of ethnocentrism. “Let some countries keep their traditions,” argues one. “Not everything needs to be modernized.”

Japanese pundits who support the revision have also emphasized “Japanese tradition.” They acknowledge that there have been female emperors (six in ancient times and two in the Edo period) but point out that they were all connected to the imperial family patrilineally; matrilineal succession was never permitted. They further reject the possibility of installing female offspring in the male line on the grounds that it would open the door to matrilineal succession.

The readership of the multilingual website Nippon.com includes both Japanese and foreign nationals. Let us know—what are your views on the issue?

Japan’s Bilateral Tradition

I have long taken issue with the assumption that patrilineal descent (male-line succession) is an indigenous Japanese tradition. To the contrary, a preference for patrilineal succession within the imperial household emerged from the Sinicization of the Japanese monarchy.

I am a family sociologist by training, and I have used the methods of historical demography to study the Japanese family from the Edo period (1603–1868) through the early Meiji era (1868–1912). During that time period, roughly one out of every five Japanese men was adopted by another family, and more than half of those adopted males were muko-yōshi, or adopted sons-in-law.(*1) The custom of adopting a son-in-law, a means of ensuring the continuity of the family line through the female line, was all but obligatory among households with daughters but no biological sons old enough to succeed to headship of the family. Nonmarital adoption was the rule among households with neither eligible sons nor daughters. In the latter case, a son was often chosen from among male relatives on the mother’s side. (At other times, the adopted heir might be a complete stranger.)

This freedom from rigid patrilineal descent is a traditional characteristic of the Japanese family. It often comes as a surprise to people from China or Korea, where succession—including by adoption—was traditionally limited to male relatives with the same surname.

It might be supposed that, within the class society of the Edo period, such expedient flexibility was limited to commoners, such as farmers, merchants, and artisans. Surely the ruling warrior class, with its emphasis on Confucian values, was more rigidly patrilineal? To put such doubts to rest, let me introduce Tsubouchi Reiko’s groundbreaking 2001 study Keishō no jinkō shakaigaku—dare ga “ie” o tsuida ka (The Population Sociology of Succession: Who Inherited the Household?). This is a work of historical demography based on a quantitative analysis of the genealogies of samurai households as recorded by various han (hereditary domains) during the Edo period. While the premodern samurai are said to have adhered to the principle of primogeniture (succession by the eldest son), this book highlights the complementary system that functioned in families with no biological male son. Tsubouchi’s research reveals that, among those who met the demographic condition of having daughters but no sons, more than 60% adopted a son-in-law, while around 10%–30% adopted a son outside of marriage. Even within the warrior class, adherence to the patrilineal norm of male-line male-only succession was not very strict.

Princess Aiko’s popularity is only part of the reason some 85% of Japanese adults currently support the recognition of a female emperor. A deeper factor informing this viewpoint is the longstanding tradition that generations of Japanese people have witnessed or experienced themselves.

Lineal Flexibility in Peripheral Societies

Let us broaden our historical perspective.

The French historical demographer and anthropologist Emmanuel Todd has posited that dual-lineage societies were once widespread across the Eurasian continent. These are societies that trace both the male and female lineages, instead of focusing on one at the expense of the other. The clans of prehistoric and early ancient Japan are believed to have preserved such a system. Women account for a significant portion of rulers interred in Japan’s burial mounds during the Kofun period (third century to early seventh century); Himiko, referred to in ancient Chinese records as the ruler of Yamatai, was no exception. Moreover, half of the emperors who reigned during the Nara period (710–794) were women.

As Todd explains it, patrilineal systems were the rule among the great civilizations of the Eurasian interior, including China, India, and the empires of West Asia (in part, it has been suggested, because they were more successful at war and aggression). As Todd explains it, the history of the family is defined by the retreat of dual-lineage societies to the continental periphery as the patriarchal systems of the great civilizations prevailed, whether through invasion or through cultural dominance.(*2) My extensive research into the Asian family has led me to the same conclusion.

In Japan, the adoption of the Ritsuryō system of government (originating in Tang-dynasty (618–907) China) triggered a gradual shift toward patrilineal descent among the leading clans. Yet matrilocal customs (the practice of residing with the wife’s family after marriage) continued among the aristocrats of the Heian period (794–1185). Matrilateral relationships remained very important and influential into the late Heian and Kamakura period (1185–1333), as seen in the powerful Fujiwara and Hōjō clans.

Moreover, the shift toward male-line succession was never fully embraced by the general populace. The traditional system of dual-lineage descent lived on in the customs of the common people. The importation of social norms and practices from more “advanced” civilizations often begins among the upper classes. When the customs of a society’s upper echelon diverge from those of the common folk, it is probably a mistake to assume that the former are more representative of that society’s indigenous traditions.

Japan was not the only country subject to the “patrilinealizing” pressure of Chinese civilization. On the Korean Peninsula, matrilocal marriage continued through the Goryeo period (935–1392), but it retreated during the Joseon period (1392–1897), amid the rapid spread of Confucianism. To ensure the purity of the patrilineal line, Korean widows were admonished not to remarry and in some cases even encouraged to follow their husbands to the grave. In Japan, by contrast, it remained relatively easy for women to divorce and remarry. Compared with Korea, Japan was separated from the Asian continent and thus more insulated from China’s direct influence. Like societies on Europe’s western edge, Japan sustained its tradition of dual-lineage descent even as patrilineal norms came to dominate. The survival of bilateral descent in these peripheral regions is evidenced by the periodic emergence of female monarchs.

Beyond the Confucian Patriarchy

Japan’s national identity is not easily defined. In the Edo period, scholars in the emerging field of Japanese studies, represented by Motoori Norinaga (1730–1801) and Hirata Atsutane (1776–1843), drew a distinction between the indigenous Japanese spirit (yamato-gokoro), and the character of imported Chinese-derived norms and forms (kara-gokoro). One difference they emphasized was the indigenous Japanese tradition of recognizing the female line. By contrast, the roughly contemporaneous school of Mitogaku, rooted in Confucianism, insisted on the principle of patrilineal succession. The historians of this school insisted that the third-century empress Jingū be referred to as kōgō (imperial consort) instead of sharing the more exalted title of tennō with Japan’s male emperors, legendary and historical.(*3)

Mitogaku held sway over the government following the Meiji Restoration, with the result that the Imperial House Law codified the rule—previously unknown in Japan—that only male offspring in the male line could succeed to the throne. The image of a male emperor also suited a modern state anxious to augment its international clout, including its military might. The spirit of the modern Japanese empire was embodied in the image of Emperor Meiji, posed on horseback and dressed in a Western-style military uniform, replacing the emperor’s traditional Japanese court robes.

No society has one simple, monolithic identity. One might best think of our national identity as a composite of overlapping, interacting layers, each deriving from different historical circumstances: a fundamental kinship structure overlaid with elements imported from a nearby great civilization and further reorganized on the model of a modern nation-state, for example.

However, the tendency among today’s conservatives, wherever they are, is to focus on the great-civilization component of national identity, including the associated religious or ethical system. Unfortunately, this layer is almost always patriarchal—and hence patrilineal—in nature. Japan is no exception. This is why the imperial household is now legally bound by an uncharacteristically inflexible patrilineal rule of succession.

But this trend poses a dilemma for Japan, situated as it is on the periphery of the Chinese civilizational sphere. Patrilinealization means Sinicization. Accepting that means positioning ourselves within China’s sphere of influence in today’s unstable world order. Historically, Japan has absorbed many elements of Chinese civilization and culture, from chopsticks and tōfu to kanji and literature. But we do not want to absorb the entire package, including autocracy and male supremacy. To survive the restructuring of the global order currently underway, we would do better to seek our own complex identity in the uniquely flexible traditions of our own multilayered society, remaining conscious of the possibilities for connections with other cultural spheres.

(Originally published in Japanese on August 20, 2026. Banner photo: Imperial family members at the New Year public greetings at the Imperial Palace on January 2, 2026. From left to right, Princess Aiko, the daughter of Emperor Naruhito, Princess Kako, the second daughter of Crown Prince Fumihito; and her younger brother Prince Hisahito, who is second in line to the throne. © Sankei Visual.)

(*1) ^ Kurosu Satomi and Ochiai Emiko, “Adoption as an Heirship Strategy under Demographic Constraints: A Case from Nineteenth-Century Japan,” Journal of Family History, 20-3, pp. 261–88.

(*2) ^ Emmanuel Todd, L’origine des systèmes familiaux (The Origins of Family Systems) (Paris: Gallimard, 2011).

(*3) ^ Empress Jingū is a semi-legendary figure whose historical existence is a point of controversy. She was said to be the consort of Emperor Chūai—regarded as the fourteenth emperor according to the official order of succession—and the mother of Emperor Ōjin. Following Chūai’s death, she is said to have ruled the country for 69 years before her son ascended the throne. Although originally treated as Japan’s fifteenth emperor, she was removed from the official order of succession under the Imperial Lineage Register Ordinance of 1926.

Japan’s Bilateral Tradition

I have long taken issue with the assumption that patrilineal descent (male-line succession) is an indigenous Japanese tradition. To the contrary, a preference for patrilineal succession within the imperial household emerged from the Sinicization of the Japanese monarchy.

I am a family sociologist by training, and I have used the methods of historical demography to study the Japanese family from the Edo period (1603–1868) through the early Meiji era (1868–1912). During that time period, roughly one out of every five Japanese men was adopted by another family, and more than half of those adopted males were muko-yōshi, or adopted sons-in-law.(*1) The custom of adopting a son-in-law, a means of ensuring the continuity of the family line through the female line, was all but obligatory among households with daughters but no biological sons old enough to succeed to headship of the family. Nonmarital adoption was the rule among households with neither eligible sons nor daughters. In the latter case, a son was often chosen from among male relatives on the mother’s side. (At other times, the adopted heir might be a complete stranger.)

This freedom from rigid patrilineal descent is a traditional characteristic of the Japanese family. It often comes as a surprise to people from China or Korea, where succession—including by adoption—was traditionally limited to male relatives with the same surname.
https://www.nippon.com/en/ncommon/contents/in-depth/3067625/3067625.jpg

It might be supposed that, within the class society of the Edo period, such expedient flexibility was limited to commoners, such as farmers, merchants, and artisans. Surely the ruling warrior class, with its emphasis on Confucian values, was more rigidly patrilineal? To put such doubts to rest, let me introduce Tsubouchi Reiko’s groundbreaking 2001 study Keishō no jinkō shakaigaku—dare ga “ie” o tsuida ka (The Population Sociology of Succession: Who Inherited the Household?). This is a work of historical demography based on a quantitative analysis of the genealogies of samurai households as recorded by various han (hereditary domains) during the Edo period. While the premodern samurai are said to have adhered to the principle of primogeniture (succession by the eldest son), this book highlights the complementary system that functioned in families with no biological male son. Tsubouchi’s research reveals that, among those who met the demographic condition of having daughters but no sons, more than 60% adopted a son-in-law, while around 10%–30% adopted a son outside of marriage. Even within the warrior class, adherence to the patrilineal norm of male-line male-only succession was not very strict.

Princess Aiko’s popularity is only part of the reason some 85% of Japanese adults currently support the recognition of a female emperor. A deeper factor informing this viewpoint is the longstanding tradition that generations of Japanese people have witnessed or experienced themselves.
Lineal Flexibility in Peripheral Societies
Let us broaden our historical perspective.

The French historical demographer and anthropologist Emmanuel Todd has posited that dual-lineage societies were once widespread across the Eurasian continent. These are societies that trace both the male and female lineages, instead of focusing on one at the expense of the other. The clans of prehistoric and early ancient Japan are believed to have preserved such a system. Women account for a significant portion of rulers interred in Japan’s burial mounds during the Kofun period (third century to early seventh century); Himiko, referred to in ancient Chinese records as the ruler of Yamatai, was no exception. Moreover, half of the emperors who reigned during the Nara period (710–794) were women.

As Todd explains it, patrilineal systems were the rule among the great civilizations of the Eurasian interior, including China, India, and the empires of West Asia (in part, it has been suggested, because they were more successful at war and aggression). As Todd explains it, the history of the family is defined by the retreat of dual-lineage societies to the continental periphery as the patriarchal systems of the great civilizations prevailed, whether through invasion or through cultural dominance.(*2) My extensive research into the Asian family has led me to the same conclusion.

In Japan, the adoption of the Ritsuryō system of government (originating in Tang-dynasty (618–907) China) triggered a gradual shift toward patrilineal descent among the leading clans. Yet matrilocal customs (the practice of residing with the wife’s family after marriage) continued among the aristocrats of the Heian period (794–1185). Matrilateral relationships remained very important and influential into the late Heian and Kamakura period (1185–1333), as seen in the powerful Fujiwara and Hōjō clans.

Moreover, the shift toward male-line succession was never fully embraced by the general populace. The traditional system of dual-lineage descent lived on in the customs of the common people. The importation of social norms and practices from more “advanced” civilizations often begins among the upper classes. When the customs of a society’s upper echelon diverge from those of the common folk, it is probably a mistake to assume that the former are more representative of that society’s indigenous traditions.

Japan was not the only country subject to the “patrilinealizing” pressure of Chinese civilization. On the Korean Peninsula, matrilocal marriage continued through the Goryeo period (935–1392), but it retreated during the Joseon period (1392–1897), amid the rapid spread of Confucianism. To ensure the purity of the patrilineal line, Korean widows were admonished not to remarry and in some cases even encouraged to follow their husbands to the grave. In Japan, by contrast, it remained relatively easy for women to divorce and remarry. Compared with Korea, Japan was separated from the Asian continent and thus more insulated from China’s direct influence. Like societies on Europe’s western edge, Japan sustained its tradition of dual-lineage descent even as patrilineal norms came to dominate. The survival of bilateral descent in these peripheral regions is evidenced by the periodic emergence of female monarchs.
Beyond the Confucian Patriarchy

Japan’s national identity is not easily defined. In the Edo period, scholars in the emerging field of Japanese studies, represented by Motoori Norinaga (1730–1801) and Hirata Atsutane (1776–1843), drew a distinction between the indigenous Japanese spirit (yamato-gokoro), and the character of imported Chinese-derived norms and forms (kara-gokoro). One difference they emphasized was the indigenous Japanese tradition of recognizing the female line. By contrast, the roughly contemporaneous school of Mitogaku, rooted in Confucianism, insisted on the principle of patrilineal succession. The historians of this school insisted that the third-century empress Jingū be referred to as kōgō (imperial consort) instead of sharing the more exalted title of tennō with Japan’s male emperors, legendary and historical.(*3)

Mitogaku held sway over the government following the Meiji Restoration, with the result that the Imperial House Law codified the rule—previously unknown in Japan—that only male offspring in the male line could succeed to the throne. The image of a male emperor also suited a modern state anxious to augment its international clout, including its military might. The spirit of the modern Japanese empire was embodied in the image of Emperor Meiji, posed on horseback and dressed in a Western-style military uniform, replacing the emperor’s traditional Japanese court robes.

No society has one simple, monolithic identity. One might best think of our national identity as a composite of overlapping, interacting layers, each deriving from different historical circumstances: a fundamental kinship structure overlaid with elements imported from a nearby great civilization and further reorganized on the model of a modern nation-state, for example.

However, the tendency among today’s conservatives, wherever they are, is to focus on the great-civilization component of national identity, including the associated religious or ethical system. Unfortunately, this layer is almost always patriarchal—and hence patrilineal—in nature. Japan is no exception. This is why the imperial household is now legally bound by an uncharacteristically inflexible patrilineal rule of succession.

But this trend poses a dilemma for Japan, situated as it is on the periphery of the Chinese civilizational sphere. Patrilinealization means Sinicization. Accepting that means positioning ourselves within China’s sphere of influence in today’s unstable world order. Historically, Japan has absorbed many elements of Chinese civilization and culture, from chopsticks and tōfu to kanji and literature. But we do not want to absorb the entire package, including autocracy and male supremacy. To survive the restructuring of the global order currently underway, we would do better to seek our own complex identity in the uniquely flexible traditions of our own multilayered society, remaining conscious of the possibilities for connections with other cultural spheres.

(Originally published in Japanese on August 20, 2026. Banner photo: Imperial family members at the New Year public greetings at the Imperial Palace on January 2, 2026. From left to right, Princess Aiko, the daughter of Emperor Naruhito, Princess Kako, the second daughter of Crown Prince Fumihito; and her younger brother Prince Hisahito, who is second in line to the throne. © Sankei Visual.)
(*1) ^ Kurosu Satomi and Ochiai Emiko, “Adoption as an Heirship Strategy under Demographic Constraints: A Case from Nineteenth-Century Japan,” Journal of Family History, 20-3, pp. 261–88.
(*2) ^ Emmanuel Todd, L’origine des systèmes familiaux (The Origins of Family Systems) (Paris: Gallimard, 2011).

(*3) ^ Empress Jingū is a semi-legendary figure whose historical existence is a point of controversy. She was said to be the consort of Emperor Chūai—regarded as the fourteenth emperor according to the official order of succession—and the mother of Emperor Ōjin. Following Chūai’s death, she is said to have ruled the country for 69 years before her son ascended the throne. Although originally treated as Japan’s fifteenth emperor, she was removed from the official order of succession under the Imperial Lineage Register Ordinance of 1926.

items.title: Unusual Picnic Places Around the World
items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: There’s nothing quite like a picnic surrounded by friends and family, soaking in the sun, sharing snacks, and enjoying the sounds of nature. Whether you prefer
items.text:
There’s nothing quite like a picnic surrounded by friends and family, soaking in the sun, sharing snacks, and enjoying the sounds of nature. Whether you prefer to use one big blanket, sit at a table with benches, or plop right onto the grass, it’s the perfect good-weather get together (and a great excuse to load up on delicious food).


With this guide, you’ll find a picnic spot that’s guaranteed to impress your guests and spark envy in your enemies. These aren’t your average grassy fields; they’re oases colored by folklore stories, whimsical art, monumental moments in history, and otherworldly formations. From an abandoned power plant in the mountains of Mexico to a gold-mine-turned-swimming-hole in southern Australia, these are the best places across the globe for an unforgettable outdoor meal.

1. Old Zoo Picnic Area 📍 Los Angeles, California


The first Los Angeles Zoo may have closed in the 1960s, but remnants still remain in Griffith Park, where they’re now outfitted with picnic tables and grills. Peek inside abandoned monkey cages and walk through the bear grotto in between bites, or wander a trail up from the caves for a view of what was once the lion dens.

2. Sports City 📍 Amman, Jordan


This crumbling sporting complex, once the training ground for elite athletes, now consists of drained swimming pools, empty gymnasiums, and overgrown tracks. However, that doesn’t mean it’s gone unused; in a city where public green space is a rarity, the complex has become a popular spot for picnics, hookah smoking, and simply sprawling in the shade.

3. Ras Angela 📍 Ras Angela, Tunisia


The rocky head of Ras Angela, or Cape Angela, juts out into the Mediterranean Sea, forming what is considered to the northernmost point of Africa. Marked with a Tunisian flag and a sculpture of the continent, it is a peaceful spot to enjoy a picnic and ocean views. You can also lay out your towel on the adjacent sandy beach and take a dip into the perfectly blue water.

4. Bomi Blue Lake 📍 Tubmanburg, Liberia


When the Liberia Mining Company abandoned its operations here in the late 1970s, it left behind a series of pit mines, which eventually filled with spring water to become a single beautiful lake. With clear, unpolluted waters, the lake is open for swimming, and the wooden pavilions around its perimeter are great for picnics.


5. Christy Buchanan’s SHE Garden & Gallery 📍 Winnsboro, South Carolina


This whimsical folk garden was created by artist and architect Christy Buchanan, who dreamed up a space that would reflect the nuanced beauty of everyday found objects. Visitors can have a picnic in the Love Shack, take pictures under the bicycle arch, or commune with ancestors in the Tiki hut. Buchanan also constantly adds to the site, so you’re sure to spy new works each time you visit. If her SUV (nicknamed Happy) is in the yard, Buchanan is home, but feel free to stop by even if she isn’t.


6. Old Wardour Castle 📍 Tisbury, England


After being decimated in a 1642 siege, this castle’s military career ended; however, it has found a second life as a tourist attraction. Fully restored and transformed with neat landscaping, the estate is now a favorite spot for picnics, weddings, and even film crews. Visitors to the castle can still climb the worn tower stairs for a sweeping view of the English countryside or lounge in the same sun-soaked courtyard that English barons once frequented.

7. Woolshed Falls 📍 Beechworth, Australia


Once the center of a massive, 19th-century mining enterprise, these falls have since been reclaimed by nature, with channels worn into the rock forming natural showers, baths and waterslides. There’s also a plunge pool at the end of the falls, unusually deep for its size thanks to the large amount of gold removed from the silty bottom.


Accessible by two different walking paths, the falls are a pleasant, family-friendly spot for picnics, swimming, and rock jumping (though children should be closely supervised).

8. Tuzluca Salt Mines 📍 Tuzluca, Turkey


The Tuz Mağarası, or Tuzluca Salt Caves, have supplied salt to this region since medieval times, though they only recently opened to the public. Now, anyone who’s not too claustrophobic can walk a boardwalk through the curving, cavernous interior. Warm lighting lends the dark space a cozy atmosphere, and picnic tables set around the chamber walls invite visitors to set up camp and stay a while.


9. Gravelly Point Park 📍 Arlington, Virginia


Most aircraft approaching Washington National Airport loop over this small Arlington park in their final descent, and locals gather for the spectacle of roaring engines, screeching wheels, and the unmistakable scent of burnt rubber on the runway. With plenty of wide open space for kids to run around and close-up views of the Potomac River, Gravelly Point is the perfect place to spend an afternoon munching on snacks and staring up at the clouds.


10. La Planta 📍 San Agustín Etla, Mexico


On the mountainside above San Agustín Etla, this former water-powered electric power plant is now a popular spot for hikers and picnickers to take in sweeping views of the city. A poem posted near the ruins reminds visitors of the importance of nature, proposing that the Earth’s resources are significantly more valuable than money: “Only after the last tree is cut ... only after the last river is poisoned ... only after the last fish is caught ... only then, you will understand ... that you cannot eat money.”

11. Al Wathba Fossil Dunes 📍 Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates


This area on the outskirts of Abu Dhabi was once covered by water. However, over time, as sediments settled at the bottom, the many mineral-heavy layers became compacted and cemented into stable structures. Since then, they’ve been further molded by winds and sediment into utterly unique shapes.


This seemingly-endless desert landscape is popular for early-morning picnics and also makes for a great camping spot. Just remember: The sand figures are incredibly fragile, so under no circumstances should you climb them.


12. Tiger Cave 📍 Mahabalipuram, India


Surrounded by swaying casuarina trees in the Bay of Bengal, Tiger Cave has long been a favored recreation spot among locals willing to make trek there from town. The site’s name comes from its crown of 11 tiger-esque heads carved around the entrance to its gaping maw. Archaeologists believe that the site likely once served as a portico from which rulers spoke or observed festivities.


The park’s grounds are maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India as a free, public space, and between its lush greenery and food and drink stands, it’s a pleasant spot for those seeking respite from Mahabalipuram’s busy streets.


13. Sa Stiddiosa 📍 Gadoni, Italy


A hike through the heart of Sardinia will lead you to this gentle waterfall, though its name actually translates from the Sardo dialect to “dripping” rather than “falling.” Local families descend into the valley to picnic, bathe in the Flumendosa River’s cool, shaded waters, and jump off the large boulder at the river’s center.


14. The Dick Lane Velodrome 📍 East Point, Georgia


Atlanta’s hub for all things cycling is a 1/5-mile track with 36-degree banked turns, which intrepid competitors race down at 40 miles an hour. Located in the city’s East Point neighborhood, the Velodrome has become a point of civic pride and local entertainment with its concession stand, public seating, picnic area, and plentiful green space. The East Point Velodrome Association runs activities on-site throughout the year, from bike safety clinics to a youth cycling league.

items.title: 12 Sculptures Made From Recycled Materials
items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: For time immemorial, human beings have generated trash ... lots and lots of trash. And from the aqueducts and municipal dumps of ancient times to the massive
items.text:
For time immemorial, human beings have generated trash ... lots and lots of trash. And from the aqueducts and municipal dumps of ancient times to the massive landfills of today, we’ve tried all kinds of ways to get rid of it. However, when trash makes its way into the right hands, it can be turned from mere waste into something imaginative and daring. Creative folks around the world have seen old materials as more than just their previous lives, looking instead to their futures.


These works show the truth of that age-old statement: “One man’s trash is another man’s treasure.” With materials ranging from old cars to scrap metal to glass bottles and discarded beach chairs, artists have gone above and beyond to reimagine how waste is thought about and used. Some projects, like a giant whale made out of polyethylene in New Mexico, are direct calls to action to reduce our footprint on the Earth. Others, such as a homestead full of sculptures built from ship parts, were simply designed on a whim by their creators. All of them showcase the innate power of outsider art to surprise and inspire us.


What Is Recycled Art?


Also called upcycled or eco-art, this practice involves turning everyday waste like plastic, glass, metal, textiles, and paper into creative works. Materials that would normally end up in landfills are, instead, transformed into imaginative forms that compel us to rethink our ideas of worth and beauty.

1. Tire Sculptures of Breighner’s Tire Center 📍 Littlestown, Pennsylvania


When Noah Russell, an employee at Breighner’s Tire Center, was challenged by his boss to build a tire float for a local parade, he created a massive lion that won first place. Riding this high, he entered the following year with an eight-foot-tall, fire-breathing dragon made out of coat hangers, turf tires, and a can of bucane.(Unsurprisingly, he won again.)


Russell followed these creations with an intricate headless horseman, a horned stag, and a reef with several aquatic animals. Along with the two prize-winning creatures, these spectacles now sit in front of Breighner’s storefront, where they’ve become a favorite landmark for people traveling along Hanover Pike.

2. Frontera Sculpture Oasis 📍 Luna County, New Mexico


This unique sculpture garden sits in the middle of the Chihuahuan desert, right on the U.S./Mexico border. Artist Taras Mychalewych created the work as a tribute to Mother Earth after his car blew up in the very same desert while he was on a cross-country drive.


The garden’s makeshift biosphere is formed out of scavenged and donated materials, from bricks to bottles, and was designed to mingle with the surrounding agave and cholla. One colorful display represents a regional mariachi band, welcoming people to the borderlands, while another portion feels directly inspired by Los Angeles’s Watts Towers. In its entirety, the isolated oasis acts as an ode to nature’s bounty but also a warning to those who have defiled it in the name of profit.

3. Rainbow Sea Container 📍 Fremantle, Australia


Situated between two bridges in a Perth suburb, this colorful sculpture pays homage to the area’s rich history as an industrial port. Locally nicknamed “The Containbow,” the nine sea containers are assembled into a striking, 29-foot-tall arch that can be spotted far and wide. Perth artist Marcus Cannin painted the containers all shades of the rainbow to recognize Fremont’s recently revitalized creative scene.

4. Badaren - Spår av Mänsklighet (The Swimmer - Traces of Man) 📍 Skanör med Falsterbo, Sweden


Nearly 200 discarded chairs and parasols, plus heaps of trash from nearby beaches, form this sculpture in a parking lot in southern Sweden. The installation serves as a reminder of the impact a single individual’s actions can have on the environment. Every single step of the lifecycle of the goods, from manufacturing to shipping and destruction, leaves an impact.

5. Volkswagen Spider Sculpture 📍 Palm Springs, California


This giant metal spider with a Volkswagen Beetle body stands outside Hole in the Wall, a former auto repair shop that’s now a hub of delightful desert eccentricity. The 28-foot-tall beast was built by Robert Miner, the shop’s longtime owner, who eventually moved onto the property and installed a treehouse/lookout tower (bedecked with spider/web motifs, naturally).

6. The Raven’s Nest 📍 Reykjavik, Iceland


On the outskirts of Iceland’s capital stand mammoth sculptures of discarded scrap metal, constantly evolving as new pieces are added. These are the work of Icelandic filmmaker Hrafn Gunnlaugsson, who bought the oceanside property in 1977 and immediately began transforming it into a surreal sculpture park.


“I was given the name Hrafn. That means raven, I think it goes with the name: Ravens like to collect things. Maybe I can blame the habit on my name,” Hafrn said of his unique hobby.


Gunnlaugsson’s home (itself a work of art) sits at the center of the site, looking out onto rusty Viking warriors, deities from around the world, totem poles formed from old ship parts, and a giant eyeball made out of a buoy.

7. Schaefer’s Auto Art 📍 Erie, Pennsylvania


For over 25 years, this roadside attraction has charmed visitors with its folksy sculptures, depicting everything from a bumblebee to an “automan” to a two-headed dinosaur. With these reimagined automobiles, Erie local Richard Schaefer has turned an otherwise quiet country road into a must-see attraction.

8. Blenko Man 📍 Weston, West Virginia


When the Museum of American Glass reopened in 2007 in a new location, this silica fellow became its mighty mascot. Rock Wilson, an avid collector of Blenko glass, commissioned renowned sculptor John Zidek to turn his collection into a tribute to West Virginia’s once-ubiquitous industry. Thus, Blenko Man was born.


As guardian and greeter for the museum, Blenko Man oversees a vast collection of practically every type of glass item imaginable, from a five-foot-tall stained glass dollhouse to a marble made in the first century AD. While he does, in fact, have two right feet (a manufacturing quirk in the original glassware used), this has just made him all the more iconic.

9. Ernesto Che Guevara Statue 📍 El Alto, Bolivia


In the very country where Che Guevara met his demise stands a 30-foot-tall statue of the dictator made out of engines, cogs, wheels, and other mechanical spare parts. Sculptor Felix Duran imbued the work with two unique features: First, Guevara is depicted stomping on a bald eagle (a clear allusion to his anti-American sentiments). Second, his face is distinctly indigenous. This latter choice has been interpreted in different ways; some view it as a cultural tribute, while others see it as the appropriation of local identity.

10. Árbol de la Sidra 📍 Gijón, Spain


Asturias, an autonomous community in northern Spain, is known for its traditional tart apple cider, served with great finesse at the region’s many sidrerías. In 2013, this artistic homage to the boozy beverage was unveiled in Gijón, where it is illuminated each night by a large lamp inside of it. According to a plaque near the sculpture, this unusual monument is a nod to the tree of life, as well as a visual representation of how natural resources can be preserved by reusing everyday objects.

11. Ethyl the Whale 📍 Santa Fe, New Mexico


At 82 feet long, this friendly whale holds the Guinness World Record for largest recycled plastic sculpture. Named for her polyethylene body, she was designed by two San Francisco artists, Yustina Salnikova and Joel Stockdill, to spread awareness of the negative impact plastics have on the environment.

12. Recycled Roadrunner Statue 📍 Las Cruces, New Mexico


At a scenic rest area, this massive roadrunner perches on a boulder, gazing over the city below. The sculpture is a whopping 20 feet tall and composed of old shoes, cell phones, bike parts, and other recycled materials. Designed by local artist Olin Calk in 1993, it first stood at the local landfill to draw attention to our poor consumption habits.

blocks.x: For time immemorial, human beings have generated trash ... lots and lots of trash. And from the aqueducts and municipal dumps of ancient times to the massive landfills of today, we’ve tried all kinds of ways to get rid of it. However, when trash makes its way into the right hands, it can be turned from mere waste into something imaginative and daring. Creative folks around the world have seen old materials as more than just their previous lives, looking instead to their futures.

These works show the truth of that age-old statement: “One man’s trash is another man’s treasure.” With materials ranging from old cars to scrap metal to glass bottles and discarded beach chairs, artists have gone above and beyond to reimagine how waste is thought about and used. Some projects, like a giant whale made out of polyethylene in New Mexico, are direct calls to action to reduce our footprint on the Earth. Others, such as a homestead full of sculptures built from ship parts, were simply designed on a whim by their creators. All of them showcase the innate power of outsider art to surprise and inspire us.
What Is Recycled Art?

Also called upcycled or eco-art, this practice involves turning everyday waste like plastic, glass, metal, textiles, and paper into creative works. Materials that would normally end up in landfills are, instead, transformed into imaginative forms that compel us to rethink our ideas of worth and beauty.

1. Tire Sculptures of Breighner’s Tire Center 📍 Littlestown, Pennsylvania

When Noah Russell, an employee at Breighner’s Tire Center, was challenged by his boss to build a tire float for a local parade, he created a massive lion that won first place. Riding this high, he entered the following year with an eight-foot-tall, fire-breathing dragon made out of coat hangers, turf tires, and a can of bucane.(Unsurprisingly, he won again.)

Russell followed these creations with an intricate headless horseman, a horned stag, and a reef with several aquatic animals. Along with the two prize-winning creatures, these spectacles now sit in front of Breighner’s storefront, where they’ve become a favorite landmark for people traveling along Hanover Pike.
2. Frontera Sculpture Oasis 📍 Luna County, New Mexico

This unique sculpture garden sits in the middle of the Chihuahuan desert, right on the U.S./Mexico border. Artist Taras Mychalewych created the work as a tribute to Mother Earth after his car blew up in the very same desert while he was on a cross-country drive.

The garden’s makeshift biosphere is formed out of scavenged and donated materials, from bricks to bottles, and was designed to mingle with the surrounding agave and cholla. One colorful display represents a regional mariachi band, welcoming people to the borderlands, while another portion feels directly inspired by Los Angeles’s Watts Towers. In its entirety, the isolated oasis acts as an ode to nature’s bounty but also a warning to those who have defiled it in the name of profit.
3. Rainbow Sea Container 📍 Fremantle, Australia

Situated between two bridges in a Perth suburb, this colorful sculpture pays homage to the area’s rich history as an industrial port. Locally nicknamed “The Containbow,” the nine sea containers are assembled into a striking, 29-foot-tall arch that can be spotted far and wide. Perth artist Marcus Cannin painted the containers all shades of the rainbow to recognize Fremont’s recently revitalized creative scene.
4. Badaren - Spår av Mänsklighet (The Swimmer - Traces of Man) 📍 Skanör med Falsterbo, Sweden

Nearly 200 discarded chairs and parasols, plus heaps of trash from nearby beaches, form this sculpture in a parking lot in southern Sweden. The installation serves as a reminder of the impact a single individual’s actions can have on the environment. Every single step of the lifecycle of the goods, from manufacturing to shipping and destruction, leaves an impact.
5. Volkswagen Spider Sculpture 📍 Palm Springs, California

This giant metal spider with a Volkswagen Beetle body stands outside Hole in the Wall, a former auto repair shop that’s now a hub of delightful desert eccentricity.
